key_insight: Video-LLMs commonly fail to perceive basic signed image-plane motion (left/right/up/down); above‑chance answers are often due to prediction biases rather than true directional understanding — a failure the authors call “directional motion blindness.”
problem_solved: Diagnoses the gap in fundamental motion-direction perception in Video-LLMs and proposes targeted interventions to restore genuine directional understanding.
method: Construct a focused diagnostic benchmark of simple single-object videos that move strictly left, right, up, or down to isolate direction perception from other cues.
Trace motion signals through Video-LLM components to localize where directional information is lost or overridden by biases (e.g., temporal encoder vs. readout).
Introduce and evaluate corrective strategies such as motion-aware inputs (optical flow/frame-differences), bias-calibration, and motion-focused fine-tuning to recover true direction sensitivity.
impact: Fixing directional motion blindness improves fundamental temporal perception in Video-LLMs, increasing reliability for real-world tasks (robotics, navigation, surveillance) and providing concrete diagnostics and remedies for model developers and evaluators.
visual_elements: Side-by-side example: sequence of frames with an overlaid arrow showing true motion direction and the model's prediction (correct vs. biased error).
Bar chart comparing chance-level accuracy, baseline Video-LLMs, and post-intervention accuracy to illustrate improvement.
Model anatomy diagram tracing motion signal flow (input frames → temporal encoder → readout) with a highlighted failure point.
Application icons (robot arm, dashcam, security camera) annotated with why reliable direction perception matters.
paper_title: Which Way Did It Move? Diagnosing and Overcoming Directional Motion Blindness in Video-LLMs
paper_authors: Jongseo Lee, Hyuntak Lee, Sunghun Kim, Sooa Kim, Jihoon Chung
